transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-20
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~56 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel, Joanna Lin, Marco Ruiz (Redwood) — Aisha Rahman, Ben Cho, Lara Gomez, Evan Price (NovusPayments)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive on throughput and scheduler behavior under peaky payment-verification loads. Focus areas: token-bucket based priority scheduling, preemption for high-priority short requests, hot-KV cache storms and mitigation, and adaptive max_num_seqs (per-GPU/tenant). Also touched on quantization tradeoffs for on-prem A40 cluster and VPC networking considerations that affect cold-starts.

Topics covered:
- Token-bucket scheduling and per-tenant priority lanes
- Dynamic adjustment of max_num_seqs based on observed seq-length distribution
- Hot-KV cache eviction heuristics and time-decay TTLs
- Burst vs steady-state throughput tradeoffs and token limits per-second
- How quantization (int8 vs fp16) influences batch packing and GPU kernel selection
- On-prem/VPC notes: NUMA, PCIe peer latency, and private control plane implications

Transcript body:
[00:00:00] Samir: All right folks, thanks for carving out time, we'll try to keep this pretty focused. I'm Samir, AE, with Joanna our SE who will drive the deep bits.
[00:00:10] Joanna: hey! quick agenda — current pain, propose a token-bucket approach with priority lanes, then KV cache hot-shard mitigation, then adaptive max_num_seqs knobs — and we'll surface config snippets. 
[00:00:22] Evan: sounds good. we really want to avoid these spikes killing our latency SLOs, and also not blow up cost when verification requests idle.
[00:00:32] Aisha: to add, our traffic is very bursty — 20% of requests are sub-second verification calls, 60% are medium chat-like prompts, 20% are long batched analytics. so mix is painful.
[00:00:45] Ben: and note — we run on-prem A40s in a VPC with some hosts behind an NAT, so cold-starts and pcie/numa topology matter.
[00:00:58] Joanna: yep; first slide — token-bucket idea: allocate per-tenant tokens that replenish per-second and a small fast lane token pool for short requests. token-bucket enforces a steady egress, but we allow short high-priority bursts via a separate bucket.
[00:01:18] Joanna: practically, that's a few knobs: refill_rate (tokens/sec), burst_capacity, short_req_threshold_ms, and fast_lane_size. also priority decay so tenants can't hoard.
[00:01:34] Aisha: can you explain how this interacts with continuous batching? our requests come in very quickly, sometimes we get 400 qps for sub-second calls.
[00:01:44] Marco: good q — continuous batching will try to pack sequences until either max_num_seqs or a timeout window. token-bucket sits upstream of the scheduler and gates acceptance into the runtime. if the token bucket denies a request it'll either queue (if we allow) or be rejected depending on policy.
[00:02:02] Ben: so queueing could add latency — we want predictable p95s. can you leverage token timeouts to keep p95 bounded?
[00:02:11] Joanna: yes — two levers: a) you set an accept_timeout for requests to wait in the scheduler queue b) the fast lane bypasses queue up to fast_lane_size. we typically set accept_timeout for short reqs to 10-30ms to avoid queuing blowups.
[00:02:28] Evan: how about preemption — if a long generation is occupying slots, can we preempt for a higher-priority short request?
[00:02:36] Joanna: preemption is tricky at GPU level. runtime supports cooperative eviction of queued long requests (if not started) and we can prioritize new short requests at pack time. once kernels are running, we rely on model-level early-stop or token caps. so prefer scheduling guarantees: cap long-request concurrency (long_seq_slots) so they don't starve short ones.
[00:02:58] Aisha: you mentioned adaptive max_num_seqs earlier — what's the heuristic there?
[00:03:04] Joanna: adaptive max_num_seqs observes the recent sequence-length distribution and inflight GPU mem usage. simple rule: compute expected memory per seq = base_attention_state + kvcache_estimate(seq_len). then choose max_num_seqs = floor((gpu_mem * safety_factor) / expected_memory_per_seq). we update every 10s with EWMA to avoid oscillation.
[00:03:31] Ben: that makes sense, but does it thrash when we get sudden long requests?
[00:03:36] Marco: hence the safety_factor and a min/max clamp. we also use a short-term token-bucket discount that temporarily lowers max slots for new long requests during a short window to protect latency-critical lanes.
[00:03:48] Aisha: what's a good safety_factor?
[00:03:50] Joanna: 0.7 to 0.85 depending on how risk tolerant you are. for your A40s I'd start at 0.75.
[00:03:58] Evan: KV cache — our hot keys are payment templates that suddenly spike when promos run — the cache sees write storms and evictions blow up GPU memory pressure. what's the recommended eviction policy?
[00:04:10] Joanna: recommended: layered eviction. 1) Per-shard time-decay score that prefers recently used but penalizes extreme hotness; 2) Adaptively increase TTL for stable keys; 3) Penalize brand-new keys during a storm (cold-to-hot dampening). this prevents hot-shard thrash.
[00:04:29] Aisha: penalize new keys? so we drop them?
[00:04:32] Joanna: not drop immediately — we add a dampening multiplier to their score so they have to prove repeated access before getting high residency. that avoids bursts of unique keys filling the cache.
[00:04:41] Ben: any tooling we can enable to observe hot-shard behavior?
[00:04:44] Marco: yes — enable per-key access counters, tail latency per key, and a heatmap export. we recommend 1s rollup windows for production tracing when you suspect storms.
[00:04:55] Evan: quantization tradeoffs — if we move from fp16 to int8 will we gain throughput without harming quality? our models are fine-tuned for payments language.
[00:05:03] Joanna: short answer yes, but caveats. int8 reduces memory and increases batch packing but can change token-level distribution for sensitive prompts. we suggest a small eval set from your production prompts: run int8 and compare p0, p1 classification/regression metrics. also quantization-aware fine-tuning sometimes helps.
[00:05:20] Aisha: do kernel selections change? we've seen different latencies depending on sequence lengths.
[00:05:25] Joanna: yes — runtime will pick different attention kernels based on seq_len and quant mode. this is why adaptive max_num_seqs is important: longer seqs may switch to kernels with higher per-seq memory and worse packing. we track kernel hit rates in the console.
[00:05:38] Ben: on-prem network — we see cold-starts when new pods schedule, and sometimes PCIe peer jumps cause extra latency. anything to tune?
[00:05:46] Marco: for on-prem, pre-warm strategy helps: keep a small standby pool of replicas pinned to NUMA nodes. also ensure CPU pinning and hugepages are set for better mmap behavior. for PCIe variability, group pods by topology and prefer same-host placement for heavy KV cache affinity.
[00:06:05] Evan: how aggressive should we be with token refill rates? if we put it too low users complain.
[00:06:11] Joanna: tune to your golden path — short verification requests should have a slightly higher refill and separate burst bucket. start conservative: set refill so that steady-state equals your 80th percentile baseline, and fast lane handles above-80th short surges.
[00:06:25] Aisha: can Redwood do a sample config we can drop in?
[00:06:29] Samir: yes — we'll share two example profiles: conservative (safety_factor 0.8, accept_timeout 25ms, fast_lane 50 tokens) and aggressive (safety_factor 0.7, accept_timeout 10ms, fast_lane 200 tokens) — Joanna will produce notes on when to pick which.
[00:06:45] Joanna: quick note on metrics — key ones: inflight_seq_count, kb_cache_hitrate, token_bucket_rejects, p95_queue_wait, kernel_swap_rate. expose them at 1s granularity for debugging.
[00:06:58] Ben: you mentioned token_bucket_rejects — is that a hard reject or can we fallback to a cheap model?
[00:07:04] Joanna: both options exist. we often recommend a fallback path: if main model denied, route to a small distilled model hosted on cheaper hardware or to cached deterministic responses. that reduces user-visible failures.
[00:07:17] Evan: what about billing — we don't want to pay for standby too much. how does Redwood count tokens when using fast-lane or standby pods?
[00:07:24] Samir: billing is per-token for hosted. for Dedicated/Private, you pay reserved capacity plus per-token usage if burst billing is enabled. standby pools are a capacity commit conversation — we'll help size to minimize waste.
[00:07:36] Aisha: sample config excerpt?
[00:07:39] Joanna: (reads) token_buckets: - tenant_fast_lane: { refill_rate: 200, burst_capacity: 400, short_req_threshold_ms: 250 } - tenant_standard: { refill_rate: 50, burst_capacity: 100 } scheduler: { accept_timeout_ms: 20, max_num_seqs_base: 64, safety_factor: 0.75, long_seq_slots: 4, min_max_num_seqs: 8, update_interval_s: 10 } kv_cache: { shard_count: 128, eviction_policy: "time_decay+dampening", dampening_window_s: 120 }
[00:08:12] Ben: how does max_num_seqs interplay with multi-tenant packing? do you reserve per-tenant slots?
[00:08:18] Joanna: we support both modes. reservation mode pins a fraction of max_num_seqs to tenants; shared mode is first-come-first-pack but weighted by token_bucket priority. reservations are good for hard isolation.
[00:08:30] Aisha: we need soft isolation — we don't mind sharing but want guarantees for short requests.
[00:08:35] Joanna: then token buckets + fast lane + long_seq_slots cap is the right combo.
[00:08:40] Evan: can we experiment with decreasing max_num_seqs to improve p95? seems counterintuitive.
[00:08:45] Joanna: decreasing max_num_seqs reduces packing efficiency but can improve tail latency because it lowers head-of-line blocking and reduces kernel-switch jitter. it's a throughput vs latency trade. you'll want to run short A/B experiments.
[00:08:58] Ben: about instrumentation — is there a simple dashboard template?
[00:09:02] Marco: yes — we'll drop a Grafana dashboard template: token buckets, heatmaps, per-gpu mem, kernel switch rate, queue wait histogram, and per-tenant rejects over time.
[00:09:14] Aisha: any gotchas for VPC private deployments?
[00:09:17] Joanna: yes — control plane reachability affects autoscale warmup. in private infra, prefer a hybrid approach where the control plane signals but local controllers maintain short-term decisions for scheduling to avoid control-plane-induced cold starts. also KMS/HSM latencies can impact startup for encrypted KV loads.
[00:09:33] Evan: last thing — can Redwood help run a controlled load test?
[00:09:37] Samir: yes we'll provide a benchmark harness and suggested request distributions. we can even run jointly to collect kernel traces.
[00:09:44] Aisha: great. two practical requests: 1) send the example configs 2) we want the dashboard and the shell script for running the load.
[00:09:51] Samir: noted. Joanna will add quantization notes too. Marco will add logging knobs.
[00:09:58] Evan: anything else?
[00:10:01] Ben: curious — do you have any auto-tuning features that adapt token refill dynamically?
[00:10:06] Joanna: we're prototyping an autoscaler that adjusts refill_rate and fast_lane_size based on short-term consumer satisfaction signals (p95 + error rate). it's more conservative in private deployments. we can show early results in the follow-up.
[00:10:21] Aisha: thanks everyone, this was helpful — we'll run the initial tests and sync next week.

(roughly 56 minute call; remaining minutes were QA on config values and Joanna shared a short YAML snippet in chat)

End of transcript.
